About the traveller (solo trip)
Contents
Departure to Oma (Aomori)

From Nagoya IC I rode on and on along the expressways. Around Myoko I was caught in the rain. When it rains on the expressway it's hard, because you have to keep riding in it until the next service area. The view of the sea from Yoneyama SA on the Hokuriku Expressway. They say you can see Sado Island from here, but I couldn't make out anything like it.
A short break at Agano SA on the Ban-etsu Expressway. It seems to have rained a little.

Looking at Mt. Bandai, famous in Tohoku. It has been completely developed into a ski resort. Once you reach Tohoku the feeling isn't one of mountain ranges in a row like in Shinshu; most of the mountains are relatively gentle. The views are open and there are few houses, so there's a relaxed atmosphere. Time seemed to flow slowly.
A beef-tongue rice bowl at Kunimi SA. I'd had it before when I came skiing at Zao, and it was still delicious.
Looking at Mt. Iwaki, the "Fuji of Tsugaru", from Tsugaru SA. After so much rain, I hoped it would be sunny from now on.
At a service area. It rained all night, but no water got in. Still, my clothes were soaked through so I hardly slept. There were others with the same idea.
Looking at the sacred mountain of Osorezan from the city of Aomori. From here I headed for the area near the summit.

Near the top of Osorezan. Sulphur was spouting everywhere and the smell of rotten eggs hung in the air. Even the river had turned yellow. This area is apparently famous for itako (spirit mediums), and there were old houses lined up with itako signs out front.
I planned to go from near the summit through to Oma, but partway the road turned to dirt. I'd assumed it would be paved all the way, which was naive. The Hornet got completely covered in mud.
I reached the northern tip of Honshu. Offshore, Hokkaido was faintly visible. About 1,400 km since leaving Nagoya. Finally, it was time to land on Hokkaido.
Oma (Aomori) to Hakodate

The grilled hokke set meal I had at a diner in Oma. I had actually planned to eat a tuna bowl with Oma's famous line-caught tuna. Sure enough, every diner had a flag out front saying "Oma tuna". But every one of them was around 2,500 yen. That's expensive... Thinking of the rest of the trip, I gave up. The hokke set was about 800 yen. The portion was huge and it tasted exceptional.
Loading the bike onto the ferry. My heart was racing before landing in Hokkaido.

The ferry set out for Hakodate port. It's about 40 km. Not directly beneath here, but the Seikan Tunnel also runs under the Tsugaru Strait. It's hard to believe anyone dug an undersea tunnel under this strait!!
Mt. Hakodate, famous for its night view of Hakodate. At first I thought it was an island, but the city of Hakodate already spreads out behind this mountain.

Landed in Hokkaido!! The roads are really wide. Apparently it's because of the winter snow, but in summer everyone seems to drive as if there are two lanes. A little confusing. Riding down the middle would probably be a nuisance. After this I went to see my friend Koji, whom I had contacted from Aomori.
In the evening Koji took me sightseeing around Hakodate in his car. In the photo are scallops we ordered at an izakaya. Simply grilled with butter, but delicious!
The night view from Mt. Hakodate. With a 15-second exposure I got a photo like this. It was so beautiful that I lost track of time staring at it.
Koji and the night view. In front of such a beautiful night view, I think a strange tension hung between Koji and me. We were both a bit shy.

Besides the night view, we came across an interesting sight. The photo came out tilted, but this is looking from Mt. Hakodate toward Honshu. At the very back are the lights of squid-fishing boats and the night view of the mainland. And in the sky, streaks of light. Aurora!? I thought for a second, but of course you couldn't see one in a place like this. Apparently it's something called isaribi, the glow from the squid boats' lamps. Perhaps thin clouds caused a Tyndall effect; it was a very mysterious sight. I didn't think the camera would capture it, but when I set the exposure to the maximum 60 seconds it came out just as it looked to the eye.

The next morning I went to the morning market. I ordered live squid, a Hakodate speciality. All over the market there were shops selling it. Tanks like this are full of swimming squid, and when you order, the staff catch one and turn it into squid "somen" noodles. Even chopped up it still moves slightly, and when you put it in your mouth the suckers stick to your tongue. As fresh as it gets. The price was high, though, at 1,500 yen. The seafood rice bowl I ordered with it was perfect too! I realised that the charm of Hokkaido is the food that comes from its rich seas. The bowl came with crab miso soup, full of crab stock and with a refined aftertaste I could have swooned over. And refills were free!!
A hamburger shop I was taken to as a Hakodate speciality. The interior was wildly flashy, promoting Christmas in the middle of summer. Locals apparently call it "Rappi".
A souvenir photo of the two of us at Goryokaku. We're both a little embarrassed. Unfortunately, it seems you can't see the star shape unless you go up the nearby tower.
Hakodate to Sounkyo
I said goodbye to Koji, who had looked after me, and left Hakodate. The clouds looked a bit threatening. And it was cold.
From the outskirts of Hakodate I rode straight along Route 5. Before reaching Uchiura Bay, Mt. Komagatake came into view.
Looking back at Komagatake from Uchiura Bay. It seems to be a standalone volcano.
Further on, I spotted Mt. Yotei far in the distance. Its shape is exactly like Mt. Fuji.
Riding on along Route 5, I reached the foot of Mt. Yotei. The shape is like Fuji, but it differs in being covered in forest almost to the summit.
Across from Yotei are the Niseko mountains. These have been completely developed into ski resorts. I'd like to come back in winter and ski them.

I skipped the Sapporo area by expressway. Looking out over farmland near Iwamizawa. Plains spread out around here and the scenery is mostly farmland. Towns are scattered about, so it doesn't feel like untouched nature, but there's little in the way, so I could still fully feel how vast Hokkaido is.
Past Asahikawa, I looked back and the sun was about to set.
Farmland glowing in the sunset.
The sunset was beautiful. It hinted at a fine day tomorrow.

Looking at the Daisetsuzan range, faintly tinged by the sunset. Near the summits there is snow and ice. Could the highest peak on the far right of the photo be Tomuraushi? In summer 2009 there were a series of mountaineering accidents around this area. It's a deep range full of appeal, but that also means its nature is harsh.
Looking at Daisetsu from just before Sounkyo. Could that be part of Mt. Kurodake?
Sounkyo to Kushiro
Sounkyo in the morning. Rather like Kamikochi, with hotels lined up. Last night I soothed my tiredness in a hotel's free foot bath.
At Sounkyo both sides of the valley are sheer cliffs.

Ryusei Falls at Sounkyo. They say Ginga Falls is further upstream, but I didn't go there. These falls seem to be quite famous, but I didn't find them very appealing. Maybe Ginga Falls is the impressive one.
Past Sounkyo to Lake Taisetsu. Of all things, it started to rain.
Looking down on the sea of forest from Mikuni Pass. The road went on as if a brown bear could come out from anywhere. The rain only got heavier, and it was extremely cold.

The road to Nukabira. A straight road typical of Hokkaido. The road surface was drenched. I wanted to take shelter somewhere quickly, but there were no towns. On Honshu you sometimes see a dead cat at the side of the road, but on this road it was a dead deer.

Arrived at Nukabira. I was soaked by the rain, so I dashed into a hot-spring inn. The open-air bath there was really good. It felt like a bath handmade in the middle of nature, and the owner seemed proud of it.
I sheltered from the rain for a while in Ashoro too, then set off again. On the way to Kushiro, the sky began to clear. Looking up, there was a rainbow. My hopes rose.
The town of Shiranuka, where I finally came out of the interior onto the Pacific side. The road was still wet, but the sun was breaking through here and there.
A favourite shot I took on the coast. I was really, really envious.
Sunset with the Kushiro Marsh behind. Please let it be sunny tomorrow.
The Kushiro Marsh as far as the eye can see. Magnificent.
I decided to sleep by the Shin-Kushiro River. It was scary.
Kushiro to Shiretoko
When I woke up, a clear, piercing blue sky had spread out. Today, at last, was perfect touring weather.
Past Kushiro, ranches spread out beside the national road known as the Milk Road. In the distance you can see the Daisetsuzan range I rode past yesterday.
Flowers blooming on the ranch.
The Hornet, all alone.
The pastures go on forever. Along the way there was a herd of cows. Of course there are cows on a ranch, but the cow density was far too low. I thought it must be hard work for the owners.

Through the pastures to the town of Shibetsu. Across the Sea of Okhotsk you can see Kunashiri, one of the Northern Territories. You couldn't exactly swim across, but it felt about as far as Hokkaido looked from Oma.
The Shiretoko Peninsula seen from Shibetsu.
From Shibetsu toward the Notsuke Peninsula. It is Japan's largest sandspit, and the sea spreads out on both sides of this straight road.
The wildflower fields of the Notsuke Peninsula. Todo fir trees once grew thick here, but perhaps because of rising sea levels they have now withered where they stand.

From the Notsuke Peninsula, Kunashiri is only 16 km away. That's less than half the distance from Oma to Hakodate. Looking at its coast through binoculars, I could even see buildings. They say about 5,000 Russians live there, so a solution to the Northern Territories issue didn't feel realistic. On the Habomai Islands, apparently only border guards live.
At the Northern Territories centre on the Notsuke Peninsula: a stuffed bird.
A poster on display inside the centre. Apparently hit-and-run accidents involving animals never stop.
Riding straight along the coastline toward Rausu.
A grilled saury set meal at the Rausu roadside station. Maybe a little early for the season, but very tasty. With a portion this big I think it was only about 800 yen.
The shore at Rausu was covered in seagulls.
Mt. Rausu seen from the town of Rausu. An imposing mountain. From here I would cross Shiretoko Pass at its base and go across the Shiretoko Peninsula.

A deer appeared near Shiretoko Pass! I hurriedly stopped the bike and went closer. But it didn't run. Perhaps it's used to people. It was strange that a deer, which should be wary, didn't run away. Neither photo is zoomed. I got to about 1 m away. Cute.
Mt. Rausu from Shiretoko Pass. A magnificent mountain. It makes me want to climb it.
Also from the pass: the sea of forest on the Rausu side. In the distance is Kunashiri. A little of Etorofu was visible too.
Mt. Rausu once more. Beyond here toward the tip is also a sanctuary for brown bears. Sadly, I never got to see one on this trip.
Shiretoko to Wakkanai
Riding from Shiretoko Pass down to the Utoro side. Out on the Sea of Okhotsk again.
The coastline on the Utoro side. This whole area is already within the World Heritage site. In winter, drift ice is said to push in.
A huge rock called Oronko Rock in Utoro. You can climb to the top by the path on the left.
I climbed to the top of Oronko Rock. Maybe because of my recent lack of exercise, I ran out of breath. Doesn't this photo look like some kind of creature? It's been given the name Godzilla Rock.
You can't see as far as the tip of Shiretoko. To see the tip you either take a sightseeing boat or walk. If you walk, bear precautions are a must.
Monkshood growing wild at the top of Oronko Rock.
Is Godzilla going to come out!? I wondered, but nothing appeared... Still, it looks like something might be there.
Oshinkoshin Falls. Not very big.
A roadside station near the town of Shari. It also has a railway station.
Sunset over the Okhotsk.
From the Lake Saroma roadside station I walked toward the observation deck. About 40 minutes of climbing. It was tough.
My efforts paid off and I reached the observation deck. A superb view spread out.
Pastures spread out around Monbetsu too. Travelling alone, I could only take lonely photos.
The Sea of Okhotsk was deep blue no matter how far I went. In winter it must be covered in drift ice. I'd like to see that.
Squid tempura and crab tempura bought at the Oumu roadside station.
In Hokkaido, cosmos season comes a little early.
A rocky shore called Usutaibe Senjoiwa.
Grassland goes on forever.

The beautiful Beniya wildflower garden. In northern Hokkaido, wildflower fields seem to spread out on the landward side of most sandy beaches. The peak of the flowering seemed to have passed, and there was a slightly lonely atmosphere. And along the way I found a sign warning that a bear had been sighted. If I ran into one suddenly in a place like this, that would be the end.
The Esanuka Line, a road I had long planned and dreamed of riding. There was almost no traffic, and it was as if the road melted into the sky. On both sides are wildflower fields and pastures.
You can't help wanting to try something like this.
The wind farm spread across the Soya Hills. There are 54 turbines in total, which is amazing.
Is that the Cape Soya lighthouse? The hills are beautiful.

At last, I reached the northernmost point of Japan. 45 degrees north. I feel I've come a long way north, but further north still lie Sakhalin and the vast Arctic. For some reason I'm drawn enormously to the lands of the north. However cold it is, people live ordinary lives. It makes me feel how remarkable humans are.
Looking north from Cape Soya. I could faintly make out the land of Sakhalin.
Long ago, American and Japanese forces apparently fought a naval battle in the Soya Strait.
At Cape Soya there is a drift-ice museum with a freezer exhibition room at minus 12°C. Everything is stuffed.
I walked a little way up the hill.
What I ate at the northernmost point was ramen. It had an enormous scallop in it.
Wakkanai to Otaru

I also made the trip out to Cape Noshappu. There were a few less people here. Offshore is Rishiri Fuji, which I've long dreamed of. From its summit you should be able to look down on the sea in every direction. The whole volcano is an island.
The vast Sarobetsu Plain and Rishiri Island.

The Sarobetsu Plain and Rishiri Island in the lingering sunset. No words are needed to describe this view. Along with Shiretoko Pass and the Beniya wildflower garden, it was one of the places that moved me most.
A line of wind turbines across the plain. The sense of perspective is nice.
I couldn't take photos around Rumoi because of heavy rain. I somehow made it to Otaru and headed straight for a hot spring ♪
Otaru is lined with retro warehouses.
Boarding the Shin Nihonkai Ferry.
Leaving Otaru port. Saying goodbye to Hokkaido. I'm sorry to leave, but I really miss Nagoya.
Seagulls follow the ship. They seem to be after food. They had a really nasty look in their eyes. They'll even take the bread right out of your hand.
